content: Each year in the United States, approximately 900 individuals lose their lives due to injuries sustained in bicycle crashes, and over 500,000 people require treatment in emergency departments. Among these injuries, head trauma represents the most significant risk to bicyclists. Head injuries account for one-third of emergency department visits, two-thirds of hospital admissions, and three-fourths of fatalities related to bicycle crashes. Facial injuries occur at a rate nearly identical to head injuries. While it is intuitively logical that helmets would offer protection against head injuries, it is essential to establish their effectiveness in real-world scenarios. The objective of this study was to determine whether bicycle helmets reduce the risk of head, brain, and facial injuries for bicyclists of all ages involved in crashes or falls. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Sport, ERIC, NTIS, Expanded Academic Index, CINAHL, PsycINFO, Occupational Safety and Health, and Dissertations Abstracts. Additionally, reference lists from previous reviews and studies from government agencies in the United States, Europe, and Australia were examined. Experts from organizations such as the International Society for Child and Adolescent Injury Prevention, the World Injury Network, and CDC-funded Injury Control and Research Centers were also consulted. The search was last updated in November 2006. The inclusion criteria for this study required controlled studies that evaluated the impact of helmet use among bicyclists who had experienced a crash. These studies needed to ensure complete outcome ascertainment, accurate measurement of helmet use, appropriate selection of comparison groups, and control for potential biases, such as selection bias, observation bias, and confounding factors. Data extraction was performed independently by two authors. Odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals were calculated to assess the protective effect of helmets against head and facial injuries. Individual study results were presented, and findings related to head and brain injuries were further summarized using meta-analysis techniques. No randomized controlled trials were identified; however, five well-conducted case-control studies met the inclusion criteria. The findings demonstrated that helmets reduce the risk of head, brain, and severe brain injuries by 63% to 88% for bicyclists of all ages. Helmets were found to provide similar levels of protection in crashes involving motor vehicles (69%) and crashes from other causes (68%). Additionally, helmets reduced injuries to the upper and mid-facial regions by 65%. In conclusion, the evidence indicates that helmets significantly reduce the risk of head and facial injuries for bicyclists of all ages, regardless of the type of crash, including those involving motor vehicles. Responses to criticisms of these findings are addressed in the Feedback section of the study.
